# Paying only the minimum on a credit card

*Test fixture written for this repo. The numbers are illustrative.*

Credit cards make it easy to pay only the minimum each month, often 2% of the balance or $25, whichever is more. That feels affordable, but it keeps you in debt for a very long time.

The reason is interest. A typical card charges about 22% a year, which works out to just under 2% a month on whatever you still owe. Each month the interest is added to your balance. If your payment is close to the interest, most of your money goes to the bank, and the balance barely moves.

Take a balance of $5,000 at 22%. Paying the minimum, it would take over 20 years to clear, and you would pay far more in interest than you originally borrowed. Paying a fixed $200 a month instead clears the same balance in about two and a half years, with roughly $1,400 in interest.

Many people believe the minimum payment is set so that you will pay off the card in a reasonable time. It isn't. It is set so that you keep paying.

What helps? Pay a fixed amount that does not shrink as the balance falls. Pay more than the minimum whenever you can. Moving the balance to a card with a lower rate, or a 0% balance transfer, can cut the interest, but watch for transfer fees and the rate after the offer ends.

Stopping new spending on the card matters too: new purchases add to the balance faster than small payments can reduce it.
